newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Asia's energy needs seen at risk.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Asia's energy needs seen at risk.

text.p: The Asia-Pacific region's growing need for power is unlikely to be fully met due to political and economic risks which could have an impact on foreign investment in new projects, according to an industry expert.
"I don't think there's any way these demand forecasts can be met," Robert Moeller, energy specialist for management firm Booz-Allen & Hamilton said.
"I don't think people are focusing well enough on the infrastructure and distribution problems," Moeller said.

Moeller, attending a meeting of APEC energy ministers and business leaders in Sydney, also said a need for high levels of capital to build new power projects and a shortage of skilled workers to run them were also deterrents to development of the region's energy sector.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) group estimates its member economies consume about half the world's energy.

APEC expects energy consumption among its members to grow by around 2.2 percent a year to 2010, compared with only 1.0 percent a year for the area represented under the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).
"If you look at a country like China, they have to build the equivalent of one new large central power station a month," Moeller said.

Australian Resources and Energy Minister Warwick Parer said on Tuesday that about US$1.6 trillion in investment capital is needed to meet the energy growth demand of the Asia-Pacific region over the next 10 years.
"It's a figure that no governments can handle on their own," Parer said. "It will need private sector investment."
Demand in India running nearly as high as China's, Moeller said. Because of the size of China and India, the two nations "end up on everyone's radar screen," he said.
However, he said both countries have significant problems that outweigh some of the smaller countries grouped under APEC.
Delays faced by Enron Corp over gaining clearance for a US$1.2 billion power plant in India until recently stunned would-be developers of power projects in India, Moeller said.
There was also the problem of a lack of a comprehensive regulatory or legal framework in some countries that most western firms are familiar with, he said.
"As a result it ends up being quite scary when you think about a billion or multi-billion-dollar investment," he said.

When the risks of large-scale investments in the larger countries are weighed "it brings those markets down far enough to make places like Thailand and Indonesia and Malaysia also look quite attractive," he said.
Elsewhere, Japan is mostly "maxed-out" holding little interest for most investors in power projects, Moeller said.

Japanese companies are probably slightly ahead of non-Japanese companies in investing in Asia, although despite the risks, "anyone who's anyone in the international power business will be in Asia," Moeller said.
Given high expectations for growth in power in Asia, companies must make hard decisions, Moeller said.

"The great debate is - do you end up being one of the early entrants and end up with a great advantage to justify all of the cost and difficulty of getting in, or do let someone else take all that pain and then capitalise on it," Moeller said.
In nearly all instances, investors were seeking to reduce risk, Moeller said.
In China, the price of most independent power projects have electricty costing up to five times what the government charges, Moeller said.
"Someone is going to have to make a substantial subsidy to make the projects work," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
